title: The LORD Proclaims His Name and Renews the Covenant
summary: Moses cuts two new stone tablets and climbs Sinai again, and the LORD passes before him proclaiming his name: compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, forgiving, yet not leaving the guilty unpunished. God renews the covenant with commands against idolatry and for Israel's feasts and firstfruits. Moses comes down after forty days with his face shining, and afterward he veils it except when he speaks with God.
story:
The covenant sealed in chapter 24 was shattered with the tablets in chapter 32, when Israel made a golden calf at the foot of the mountain while Moses was receiving the law. Moses interceded, and God relented from destroying the people (32:11-14), but he refused to go up among them himself (33:3). Moses pleaded again, and God promised that his presence would go with them (33:14). Then Moses asked, “Please show me Your glory” (33:18), and God promised to make his goodness pass by and to proclaim his name, while warning that no one can see his face and live (33:19-23).

Chapter 34 keeps that promise. The golden calf episode ends not with Israel's repentance proving itself, but with God declaring who he is. The same God who had threatened to consume his people describes himself first as compassionate and gracious. On that basis the covenant is remade, the second set of tablets is written, and the work of building the tabernacle can begin in chapter 35. The self-description in verses 6 and 7 becomes Israel's creed about God, quoted and echoed across the rest of the Old Testament, and the chapter closes with Moses' shining face, the visible sign that God is again speaking with his people through his servant.
historical:
The setting is again the summit of Sinai, with the mountain sealed off as it was in chapter 19. The location of Mount Sinai is debated. Christian tradition since the fourth century has identified it with Jebel Musa in the south of the Sinai Peninsula, where the emperor Justinian built the fortified monastery now called St Catherine's in the sixth century; other proposals place it in the north of the peninsula or in northwest Arabia. The date of the exodus is also contested: some date it to the fifteenth century BC on the basis of 1 Kings 6:1, others to the thirteenth century BC on the basis of Exodus 1:11 and the archaeology of Egypt and Canaan.

The laws in verses 11 to 26 closely parallel the covenant laws of 23:12-19. Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, in an anonymous essay of 1773, argued that these verses, not Exodus 20, were the original contents of the tablets, and Julius Wellhausen later called them the Ritual Decalogue, in contrast to the Ethical Decalogue of chapter 20. Scholars who hold this view count ten ritual commands in different ways, and none of the proposed lists is agreed. Verse 28 says that the words of the covenant, the Ten Commandments, were written on the tablets, and the Hebrew does not name the writer; Deuteronomy 10:4 says the LORD wrote the same words that were on the first tablets. Most readers take the tablets to hold the Ten Commandments of chapter 20, with verses 10 to 26 as a restatement of key covenant duties after the calf, the ones Israel had just broken.

The warnings against Canaanite worship reflect a real and lasting temptation. Asherah was a goddess known from the Ugaritic texts of the thirteenth century BC as Athirat, consort of the high god El, and her cult object, a wooden pole or stylized tree, stood at many shrines. Inscriptions from Kuntillet Ajrud in the northeastern Sinai, from about 800 BC, bless people by the LORD of Samaria and his asherah and the LORD of Teman and his asherah, and a tomb inscription from Khirbet el-Qom near Hebron uses similar language, which shows that some Israelites later combined the worship of the LORD with hers. Standing stones (matsevot) have been found at many sites; the Israelite shrine in the fortress at Arad in the Negev had one in its inner niche. Scholars since George Mendenhall's study of 1955 have compared the covenant's demand for exclusive loyalty to the treaties of Hittite and Assyrian overlords, which forbade vassals to make alliances with other kings, a background that helps explain why a treaty with Canaan's peoples (verses 12 and 15) is treated as a betrayal of the LORD.

The month of Abib (verse 18) is an old name meaning fresh ears of grain, the season of the barley harvest in spring; after the exile the Babylonian name Nisan took its place (Nehemiah 2:1, Esther 3:7). The Gezer Calendar, a small limestone tablet from about the tenth century BC found at Gezer in 1908, lists the farming year month by month, including a month of barley harvest and a month of harvest and measuring, and shows how closely Israel's calendar followed the fields.
cultural:
Israel's worship was tied to the farming year. The Feast of Unleavened Bread came at the barley harvest in spring and remembered the exodus; the Feast of Weeks, later called Pentecost from the Greek word for fiftieth, marked the wheat harvest seven weeks later; and the Feast of Ingathering, also called Booths or Tabernacles, closed the year's harvest in autumn. At each one the men of Israel were to appear before God. Leaving farms and borders unguarded three times a year was an act of trust, which is why verse 24 promises that no one will covet their land while they are away. The Sabbath command in verse 21 adds that rest must be kept even in plowing and harvest, the two seasons when a day's work mattered most.

The firstborn of animals and sons belonged to God and had to be given or redeemed. A firstborn donkey, an unclean animal that could not be sacrificed, was redeemed with a lamb or else killed, and firstborn sons were redeemed; Numbers 18:15-16 later sets the price at five shekels, and Jewish families still keep the ceremony of pidyon haben, the redemption of the firstborn son, when the son is a month old. The rule that no one should appear before God empty-handed (verse 20) meant that worship involved a gift from the worshiper's own labor.

The command not to cook a young goat in its mother's milk (verse 26) appears three times in the Torah (23:19, Deuteronomy 14:21). Scholars once explained it as a ban on a Canaanite ritual known from a Ugaritic text, but that reading of the text is now widely doubted. Philo read it as a lesson in humaneness, like the law against taking a mother bird with her young (Deuteronomy 22:6-7), and Maimonides suggested it forbade a pagan practice (Guide of the Perplexed 3.48). The Talmud took the threefold repetition as forbidding cooking, eating, and benefiting from meat and milk together (b. Chullin 115b), the basis of the Jewish separation of meat and dairy.

The ancient Near East pictured gods and kings surrounded by a terrifying radiance, which Akkadian texts call melammu, and Israel knew the glory of the LORD as fire and cloud on the mountain (24:17). Moses' face does not produce its own light but reflects the glory of the one he has spoken with. The Hebrew verb for shine is related to the word for horn, and the Latin Vulgate translated it as horned. That rendering lies behind the tradition of the horned Moses in European art, most famously Michelangelo's statue for the tomb of Pope Julius II in Rome (about 1513 to 1515), though Ruth Mellinkoff's study The Horned Moses in Medieval Art and Thought (1970) shows that the image took centuries to appear in art and gathered other meanings along the way. The veil (masveh) is otherwise unknown, and the text does not say what it looked like.
literary:
The chapter has three movements: the theophany and God's proclamation of his name (verses 1-9), the covenant renewal and its commands (verses 10-28), and Moses' descent with a shining face (verses 29-35). It is the last part of a single story that runs from chapter 32 to chapter 34: the covenant broken, Moses' intercession, the promise of presence, and the covenant restored. Many details deliberately answer chapter 32. Moses rises early (verse 4), as the people had risen early to sacrifice to the calf (32:6); God forbids molten gods (verse 17), using the word for the molten calf (32:4); and the tablets Moses broke (32:19) are replaced by tablets he carves himself (verse 1).

The proclamation of verses 6 and 7 is balanced with care: a long list of mercies and then a short, sober note of justice, with love extended to a thousand generations and punishment limited to three or four. It expands the words of 20:5-6, where the order was reversed and judgment came first. Its phrases reappear more than any other description of God in the Old Testament: Numbers 14:18, Nehemiah 9:17, Psalms 86:15, 103:8, and 145:8, Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2, and Nahum 1:3. Each later text chooses what it needs. Joel uses the mercy to call Israel to return; Nahum uses the justice to announce Nineveh's fall; and Jonah complains about it, “I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion”, because it meant God would spare his enemies.

The covenant terms (verses 10-26) are framed by God's promise to do wonders (verse 10) and God's command to write (verse 27). The chapter's final paragraph (verses 29-35) is built on repetition: the phrase the skin of his face shone occurs three times (verses 29, 30, 35), and the veil three times (verses 33, 34, 35). The last verses shift into verbs of repeated action, describing not a single day but Moses' ongoing practice: in before the LORD unveiled, out to the people unveiled, and then veiled again.

outline.t: New tablets and a second ascent
The LORD proclaims his name, and Moses worships and pleads
The covenant renewed: no treaties and no other gods
The words of the covenant written
Moses' radiant face and the veil

doctrines.note: God answers Moses' request to see his glory by proclaiming his name, the LORD (YHWH), twice (verse 6), and by describing what that name means. Verse 14 adds that his name is Jealous. In Scripture a name discloses character, and here the name of Exodus 3:14-15 is filled out with the qualities that make it the name Israel can call on.

Asked to show his glory, God describes his character. Mercy, grace, patience, loyal love, faithfulness, and forgiveness come first and at length; justice comes last but is not removed. The Old Testament's most repeated statement about God holds love and justice together without letting either cancel the other.

Moses asked to see God's glory (33:18) and received a proclamation of God's goodness and name. When he came down, his face shone from speaking with the LORD (verse 29). The glory is not a spectacle Moses possesses but a reflection of the God he has met, which Paul takes up in 2 Corinthians 3:18.

The covenant is renewed after it has been broken, and the renewal rests on God's character rather than Israel's record. Moses' plea in verse 9 names the people as stiff-necked and asks for forgiveness on that very basis, and God answers, “Behold, I am making a covenant” (verse 10).

God's name is Jealous (verse 14): he claims Israel's exclusive worship as a husband claims his wife's faithfulness. The warnings against treaties, shared sacrifices, and intermarriage concern the pull toward other gods, which verse 16 names directly, and verse 17 forbids molten gods like the calf.

words.note: Rachum, compassionate, merciful. It occurs 13 times in the Old Testament, and in every case but one (Psalm 112:4, of the righteous person) it describes God. It is related to rechem, womb, the word in verse 19 for the firstborn that opens the womb, and to rachamim, compassion. Phyllis Trible, in God and the Rhetoric of Sexuality (1978), drew out the image of a mother's feeling for the child of her womb; a shared root does not prove that every use carries the image, but the adjective describes tender, visceral care. It stands first in God's self-description.

Channun, gracious. It occurs 13 times and is used almost only of God, usually paired with rachum (Psalm 103:8, Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2). It comes from the root chanan, to show favor, and describes kindness given freely, not earned. Moses has twice asked whether he has found favor (chen) in God's sight (33:13, 34:9), and God's first description of himself includes the answer: he is by nature one who gives favor.

Chesed, loving devotion, often translated steadfast love, lovingkindness, loyal love, or mercy. It occurs about 250 times in the Old Testament, more than half of them in the Psalms. Standard lexicons (BDB, HALOT) describe it as goodness and loyalty within a relationship, and it often means love that keeps faith when the other party has failed. Here God abounds in it (verse 6) and keeps it to a thousand generations (verse 7). It is one of the Old Testament's great words for God's character, and the refrain of Psalm 136 repeats it in every verse.

Emet, faithfulness or truth. It occurs about 127 times and describes what is firm, reliable, and trustworthy; the related word amen comes from the same root. Paired with chesed, as here and often in the Psalms (Psalm 25:10, 85:10), it means that God's love is dependable. John's description of the Word made flesh as “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14) most likely echoes this pair from Exodus 34:6.

Nasa, to lift, carry, or bear, one of the most common verbs in the Old Testament, used about 650 times. When its object is sin, it means to bear the guilt of it, or to forgive by carrying it away. In verse 7 God is nose avon vafesha vechatta'ah, forgiving (literally bearing) iniquity, transgression, and sin, the three main words for wrong in Hebrew. The same verb describes the goat of the Day of Atonement, which carries the people's iniquities into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:22), and the servant of Isaiah 53:12, who bore the sin of many.

Salach, to forgive, pardon. It occurs about 46 times, and in every case the one who forgives is God; the Old Testament never uses it of one person forgiving another. Its first appearance is Moses' prayer in verse 9, “forgive our iniquity and sin”. Moses later pleads on the basis of this chapter's words for the same pardon after the spies' report (Numbers 14:19-20), and the new covenant promise of Jeremiah 31:34 uses it: God will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no more.

Qanna, jealous, an adjective used only of God and only six times, all in the Pentateuch (20:5; 34:14, twice; Deuteronomy 4:24, 5:9, 6:15). It is not petty envy but the passionate, exclusive love that will not share a covenant partner with rivals, much as a faithful husband will not accept his wife's adultery. In verse 14 it is even called God's name, a way of saying this is essential to who he is. The related noun qin'ah can mean zeal as well as jealousy.

Qaran, to send out rays or to shine. The verb is formed from the noun qeren, horn, and occurs only four times: three times in this passage (verses 29, 30, 35) for the skin of Moses' face, and once in Psalm 69:31 of a bull that has horns. Horns and rays share the image of something projecting outward, as Habakkuk 3:4 speaks of rays from God's hand using the dual of qeren. The link explains the Latin rendering horned, but the sense in context is clearly that Moses' skin shone from being in God's presence.

christ:
John's Gospel draws on this chapter as it introduces Jesus. Moses asked to see God's glory and heard him proclaimed as abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness; John says of the Word made flesh, “We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). Grace and truth most likely render the Hebrew pair chesed and emet of verse 6. John then adds, “For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17), and “No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known” (John 1:18), an answer to Exodus 33:20, where God told Moses that no one can see his face and live. The tabernacle Moses is about to build is where God will dwell among his people, and John says the Word made his dwelling among us, using a verb related to the Greek word for tent.

Paul reads the shining face and the veil in 2 Corinthians 3. He contrasts the ministry of the covenant written on stone, which came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at Moses' face, with the greater glory of the Spirit's ministry, and he says that believers, “who with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into His image” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Paul adds that Moses veiled himself “to keep the Israelites from gazing at the end of what was fading away” (2 Corinthians 3:13), a detail Exodus does not state. Interpreters differ on how he reached it: some think he inferred it from the repeated veiling, others, such as Scott Hafemann (Paul, Moses, and the History of Israel, 1995), argue that Paul meant the veil shielded a stiff-necked people from a glory that would have judged them. Paul also borrows the turning of verse 34: as Moses removed the veil when he went in before the LORD, so “whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away” (2 Corinthians 3:16). The light that shone on Moses' face shines, Paul says, “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

The Gospels' account of the transfiguration recalls this chapter. On a mountain, Jesus' face shone like the sun (Matthew 17:2), a cloud overshadowed the disciples, and Moses himself appeared; but where Moses' face reflected a glory not his own, Jesus is revealed as the beloved Son whose glory it is. Moses' forty days without food on the mountain find an echo in Jesus' forty days of fasting in the wilderness (Matthew 4:2). And the name proclaimed in verses 6 and 7, merciful yet not clearing the guilty, is the tension the New Testament sees resolved at the cross, where God shows himself both just and the one who justifies (Romans 3:26).
interpretation:
Jewish tradition calls verses 6 and 7 the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy (shelosh esreh middot), though the ways of counting thirteen differ. The Talmud pictures God wrapping himself like a prayer leader and teaching Moses this order of prayer, promising that when Israel recites it, it will not return empty (b. Rosh Hashanah 17b). The words are said in the penitential prayers of the High Holy Day season, throughout Yom Kippur, and on festivals when the ark is opened. Jewish liturgy stops the quotation at venaqqeh, ‘and clearing’, so that it ends on acquittal, and the Talmud explains that God clears those who repent (b. Yoma 86a). The Talmud also meets the problem of verse 7 directly: it reconciles God's visiting iniquity on children with Deuteronomy 24:16 by saying that it applies when the children hold on to their fathers' deeds (b. Berakhot 7a), and Targum Onkelos makes the same point in its rendering of 20:5. On public fast days the synagogue reads 32:11-14 and 34:1-10, and the congregation says the attributes aloud at verses 6 and 7; the weekly portion Ki Tisa (30:11-34:35) is paired with Elijah on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18). Maimonides, in the Guide of the Perplexed (1.54), taught that what Moses was shown were God's ways, attributes of his action in the world, while God's essence remained beyond knowing.

Christian readers from the start heard the chapter through John 1 and 2 Corinthians 3. Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Moses read Moses' desire to see God's glory, which is answered here, as the soul's endless ascent into the God who is always more than can be seen. Jerome's Latin rendering of verse 29 as horned passed into medieval art and drama, and Ruth Mellinkoff (1970) traced the image's long and complex history. Calvin, in the Institutes (1.10.2), cited verses 6 and 7 as a brief summary of all that people can know of God, describing him not as he is in himself but as he is toward us, a point close to Maimonides', and he treated the chapter at length in his harmony of the last four books of Moses (1563). The Roman Catholic lectionary reads 34:4-6 and 8-9 on Trinity Sunday in Year A, and the Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 29 to 35 on Transfiguration Sunday in Year C, with 2 Corinthians 3 and Luke's account of the transfiguration.

Modern criticism long focused on the relation of verses 10 to 26 to chapter 20. Goethe's essay of 1773 and Julius Wellhausen's work made the Ritual Decalogue a fixture of source criticism. Brevard Childs (The Book of Exodus, 1974) and R. W. L. Moberly (At the Mountain of God, 1983) turned attention to chapters 32 to 34 as a deliberate literary and theological whole, in which the covenant is restored by God's grace to a people who remain stiff-necked. Walter Brueggemann's Theology of the Old Testament (1997) treats verses 6 and 7 as the core of Israel's testimony about God. In art, Michelangelo's horned Moses (about 1513 to 1515) and Rembrandt's Moses with the Ten Commandments (1659, Berlin) are the best-known images of the lawgiver with the tablets, and Rembrandt's painting has been read as showing either the breaking of the first tablets or the presentation of the second.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from translation choices rather than manuscripts. In verses 29, 30, and 35 the Hebrew verb qaran was rendered by the Septuagint as ‘glorified’ and by Jerome's Latin Vulgate as ‘horned’; English Bibles from the beginning have rendered it as shining. In verse 33 the King James Version's ‘till Moses had done speaking with them, he put a vail on his face’ suggests that Moses wore the veil while he spoke; modern versions read ‘when Moses had finished speaking’, which fits verses 34 and 35, where he speaks to the people unveiled. In verse 9 versions differ over the small word ki: the BSB and most others take it as concessive (‘although this is a stiff-necked people’), while some commentators, notably R. W. L. Moberly, argue for the ordinary causal sense (‘because’). In verse 28 the Hebrew does not name who wrote on the tablets, and versions either keep the ambiguous ‘he’ (BSB, ESV) or supply ‘the LORD’ or ‘Moses’.

There is one well-known point of vocalization. In verse 19 the Masoretic vowels read the consonants of ‘male’ as a verb meaning ‘it shall be remembered’, which makes poor sense; the Septuagint and most modern versions, the BSB included, read ‘all the firstborn males among your livestock’. In verses 23 and 24, and in 23:15 and 23:17, some scholars suggest that the passive vowels of ‘appear before’ (‘be seen’) replaced an original active ‘see the face of’, out of reverence; the suggestion is plausible but unprovable. The verse numbering of Exodus 34 is the same in Hebrew and English Bibles.

teach.big: When his people have broken the covenant, the LORD shows his glory by proclaiming his name, merciful and gracious yet just, and on that character alone he renews the covenant and lets his glory shine on the face of his servant.

outline.t: God restores what sin broke: the same words are written again, and the only carving he commands after the carved calf is the carving of tablets to receive his word.
The fullest answer to the request to see God's glory is a description of his character, in which mercy comes first and at length and justice is real but limited.
The right response to God's self-revelation is worship and prayer, and Moses pleads for a stiff-necked people precisely because they need God's presence most.
Renewed grace calls for renewed loyalty; the LORD whose name is Jealous will not share his people with other gods.
Worship shapes time and work: feasts, firstborn, Sabbath, and firstfruits train a people to trust God with their calendar, their children, and their harvests.
The covenant is written down; God's word, not Israel's memory or feelings, is the basis of the relationship.
Those who speak with God reflect his glory, often without knowing it, and the glory reaches the people through the word Moses brings.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first quotes only verse 6 and stops, as if the God of Exodus were only kind; the proclamation includes justice, and Nahum 1:3 quotes that half. The opposite error reads verse 7 as a curse on descendants for sins they did not commit, which Ezekiel 18:20 and Deuteronomy 24:16 rule out as a principle; the Talmud and many Christian interpreters read it of children who continue in their parents' sins, and it describes the reach of sin's consequences more than inherited guilt. A third error uses the chapter to build a contrast between an angry Old Testament God and a loving New Testament God; this chapter is the Old Testament's own central confession of God's mercy, and John 1 draws from it.

Teachers should also avoid treating verse 16 as a teaching about ethnicity. The concern is worship of other gods, as the verse says and as Ruth the Moabite shows. They should avoid making Moses' shining face a promise that spiritual people will visibly glow or be admired; the point is that Moses did not know, and the glory was God's. And they should not read Paul's contrast in 2 Corinthians 3 as a dismissal of Moses or of the Jewish people; Paul's argument depends on the real glory of the Sinai covenant.
teach.pastoral: This chapter speaks to people who believe they have failed too badly to be restored. The second tablets are given after the worst failure in Israel's early history, and God's first words about himself are compassionate and gracious. It can also press on those who carry the damage of a parent's sin, since verse 7 speaks of the third and fourth generations. Teach it with care: the text does not say that a child is guilty for a parent's abuse, addiction, or violence, but it does describe honestly how such harm travels through families, and it sets that harm within a far larger mercy that reaches a thousand generations. Those who have been taught that God is harsh or that they must earn his favor may need to hear verses 6 and 7 slowly, in the order God speaks them.

hard.q: Does God punish children for their parents' sins?
hard.a:
The objection is strongest when it comes from the Bible itself. Verse 7 says God visits the iniquity of the fathers on their children and grandchildren to the third and fourth generations. Yet Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids executing children for their parents' crimes, Jeremiah 31:29-30 looks forward to a day when people will no longer say that the fathers ate sour grapes and the children's teeth were set on edge, and Ezekiel says plainly, “A son will not bear the iniquity of his father” (Ezekiel 18:20). Many critical scholars read Deuteronomy, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel as a later correction of an older idea of collective guilt, and moral critics of the Bible cite verse 7 as an example of a divine justice that no human court would accept.

Interpreters have answered in several ways. The oldest Jewish answer, in Targum Onkelos on 20:5 and the Talmud (b. Berakhot 7a), is that the verse applies when children continue in their parents' sins, and the parallel in 20:5 supports it by adding “of those who hate Me”. A second answer, common among modern commentators, notes that three or four generations is the size of an extended household living together at one time, so the verse describes how a family's sin damages everyone under its roof rather than a curse on distant descendants. A third reads the verse as a statement about the corporate life of a people, whose sins and their consequences carry forward in history, as Israel's exile came after generations of idolatry; Joel Kaminsky's Corporate Responsibility in the Hebrew Bible (1995) argues that individual and corporate responsibility stand side by side in the Old Testament rather than one replacing the other.

The proportion also matters. Love reaches to a thousand generations; judgment stops at three or four. The verse is part of a proclamation whose main point is God's mercy. Jesus rejected the assumption that a man was born blind because of his parents' sin (John 9:2-3), which shows that the verse was never meant to explain every suffering.

hard.q: Is a God whose name is Jealous a petty or insecure God?
hard.a:
The objection is familiar. Jealousy is usually counted a vice, a sign of insecurity and possessiveness, and a God who calls himself Jealous (verse 14) and demands the destruction of other peoples' shrines (verse 13) looks to many modern readers like an intolerant tribal deity. Richard Dawkins opened the second chapter of The God Delusion (2006) by describing the God of the Old Testament as jealous and proud of it, among many harsher charges, and critics of monotheism have argued that exclusive worship breeds intolerance.

Responses begin with the word itself. Qanna and the related noun qin'ah cover both jealousy and zeal, and in the Old Testament God's jealousy is always the jealousy of a covenant partner, the anger of a faithful husband betrayed, not the envy of someone who covets what belongs to another. The prophets develop the image at length (Hosea 1 to 3, Ezekiel 16), and a love that felt nothing when betrayed would not be love. Abraham Joshua Heschel, in The Prophets (1962), argued that the biblical God is a God of pathos, moved by what his people do, and that this is a strength of biblical faith, not an embarrassment. Maimonides took a different route, treating such language as describing God's actions toward people rather than feelings in God (Guide of the Perplexed 1.54). Christian theologians have argued that exclusive worship of the one true God is good for the worshiper, since idols enslave and diminish those who serve them (Psalm 115:8). In this chapter the command to destroy shrines concerns Israel's own worship in its own land and is set beside the warning that such worship would become a snare; it is not a charter for coercing other peoples elsewhere. Readers will weigh these answers differently, but the chapter itself sets God's jealousy inside a self-description that begins with compassion and grace.

observe: What does Moses ask for in 33:18, and what does God actually show and say to him in 34:5-7?
List the qualities God names in verses 6 and 7. How many describe mercy, and how many describe justice?
Who noticed that Moses' face was shining, and when did Moses wear the veil and when did he remove it?
interpret: Why do you think God answers a request to see his glory with a description of his character rather than a vision?
How can God be both forgiving iniquity and not leaving the guilty unpunished? How do later passages such as Jonah 4:2 and Nahum 1:3 use the two halves?
Why might the renewed covenant focus on idolatry, feasts, and firstfruits rather than repeating all Ten Commandments?
apply: Which part of verses 6 and 7 do you find hardest to believe about God, and why?
Jonah was angry that God was gracious to his enemies. Whom would you be uncomfortable seeing God forgive?
Moses did not know his face was shining. What might it mean that the effects of time with God are often more visible to others than to ourselves?
